# Learn Crime Mapping with R

> An introductory textbook on using R to understand and visualise spatial and spatio-temporal patterns of crime.

Author: Matt Ashby
Edition: 2026 edition
Licence: CC BY

## Front matter

- [Learn Crime Mapping with R](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/index.llms.md): This book will give you the knowledge and skills to effectively communicate information about crime and related topics using maps. We will cover the principles of analysing geographic information and the strengths and weaknesses of different maps for communicating it.
- [Contents](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/contents.llms.md): This book is divided into 16 chapters, each covering a different topic related to crime mapping with R. Some chapters focus on mapping skills, while others focus on data wrangling or on how good coding practice can make your life easier. The chapters build on one another, so the easiest way to go through the book is to work through the chapters in order. But if you already know some R coding, and something about mapping, you might want to jump into a specific chapter to get what you need.
## Part I: Getting started

- [Install the software needed for this book](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/setup.llms.md): Before we start mapping, we need to install the software we will need to make crime maps and reports.
- [1  Getting started](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/01_getting_started/index.llms.md): Get started with crime mapping by learning about why putting crime on maps is useful, get a tour of the Positron software we will use throughout this course and learn how to keep your files organised.
- [2  Your first crime map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.llms.md): This chapter provides a beginner-friendly introduction to creating crime maps in R. We will walk through the essential steps, including loading pre-prepared crime data, processing it into a usable format, and visualising it on a map. This chapter introduces key R concepts like working with spatial data and using simple features (SF) objects. We’ll learn to distinguish between temporary and permanent code, understand the basics of coordinate reference systems, and produce a basic map. Let’s get started!
## Part II: Making a good crime map

- [3  Loading and selecting data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.llms.md): This chapter introduces the first essential skills of data wrangling: loading data into R and choosing the rows and columns needed for an analysis. We will learn how functions and packages work, how to read CSV and Excel files, how to give objects meaningful names and how to use the dplyr package to select and filter data.
- [4  Transforming and summarising data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/04_transforming_data/index.llms.md): In Chapter 3 we learned how to load tabular data and choose the rows and columns needed for an analysis. This chapter continues the data-wrangling process. We will learn how to create new columns, summarise and arrange rows, connect several operations in a pipeline and save the processed result without changing the original data.
- [5  Your second crime map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.llms.md): In Chapter 2 we learned the basics of creating a crime map in R. In this chapter we will create a second crime map, this time focusing a bit more on the details. We will learn more about working with spatial data, including how to load data and convert it into a format suitable for mapping. We will practise visualising crime data effectively by creating a clear and accurate map. Let’s dive into the process and start mapping!
- [6  Mapping crime patterns](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/06_mapping_crime_patterns/index.llms.md): This chapter introduces techniques for mapping concentrations of recorded crime using a technique called kernel density estimation (KDE). We will learn how to produce a clear density map that shows where crime is most concentrated.
- [7  Giving a map context](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.llms.md): In Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 we’ve learned how to make maps of crime data. In this chapter we’ll learn to make those maps more useful by adding context using titles, legends and other supporting elements. In particular we’ll focus on the important of visual hierarchy in guiding a reader’s attention to the most important parts of a map. We’ll also learn how to save a finished map as a file so that it can be shared with others.
## Part III: Crime maps for different purposes

- [8  Handling bugs in your code](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/08_handling_bugs/index.llms.md): In this chapter, we will learn how to identify and fix bugs in R code. We will learn how to interpret messages, warnings and errors, and how to distinguish between different types of error. The chapter also introduces a systematic debugging process that you can use to find and fix problems. We will practise diagnosing problems in code and asking others for help when we need it.
- [9  Mapping area data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/09_mapping_areas/index.llms.md): In this chapter, we will learn how to create crime maps that display data for geographic areas rather than individual crime locations. We will explore how to count crimes within predefined areas, visualize these counts using thematic maps, and understand the challenges of interpreting area-based data. We will also explore interactive maps, crime rate calculations, and important spatial concepts like the ecological fallacy.
- [10  Handling messy data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/10_messy_data/index.llms.md): Data is at the core of crime mapping, but data isn’t always provided in the best format for analysis. This chapter introduces some ways we can tidy and prepare datasets for analysis in R. This includes restructuring data, dealing with missing values, separating variables and geocoding locations. We will practise preparing common forms of messy data for analysis.
- [11  Writing reports in R](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/11_writing_reports/index.llms.md): In Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 we’ve learned how to make crime maps, but almost every analysis also needs text, charts and other things to help the audience understand the main messages. In this chapter we will learn how to use a tool called Quarto to produce structured reports in Positron and export them to multiple formats, including HTML, Word and PDF.
- [12  Using data about places](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/12_place_data/index.llms.md): Understanding the spatial context of crime is essential for effective crime mapping and analysis. This chapter explores how to make crime maps more informative by incorporating additional data about places. It covers sources of spatial data, including open data repositories and OpenStreetMap, and explains how to use shapefiles to add context to crime patterns.
- [13  Mapping hotspots](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/13_mapping_hotspots/index.llms.md): In this chapter we will learn three techniques for better understanding hotspots of crime. We will learn what a crime hotspot is and how to use R to identify hotspots and plot them on maps. We will also learn how to better understand spatial concentrations in crime risk using dual kernel density estimation.
- [14  Presenting spatial information without maps](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/14_no_maps/index.llms.md): Maps are powerful tools for visualising spatial data, but they are not always the best choice. In this chapter, we will learn to choose between maps, tables and charts, then use the ggplot2 and gt packages to communicate spatial information clearly. We will create tables, bar charts, distribution plots and scatter plots, each suited to answering a different type of question.
- [15  Mapping crime over time](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/15_mapping_time/index.llms.md): Understanding how crime varies over time is essential for effective crime analysis. This chapter introduces techniques for identifying short-term and long-term variations in crime. We will learn how to handle date and time data, visualise temporal changes, and create animated maps to illustrate crime trends dynamically.
- [16  Mapping crime series](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/16_crime_series/index.llms.md): In this chapter we will learn to map crime series, a sequence of crimes committed by the same individual or group. Using a historical case study, we will learn how to visualise crime series by mapping linked cases.
## Appendices

- [Appendix A — Functions for reading data into R](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/read_functions.llms.md): R can read data in many different formats. Different functions (often from different packages) are needed to read files of different formats. These are some of the functions needed to read common types of file used in data analysis, including spatial data formats.
- [Appendix B — Checklist: Making a good crime map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/map_checklist.llms.md): Whenever you make a crime map, use this checklist to make sure your map is likely to be useful to the people you are making it for.
- [Appendix C — Common R errors and how to fix them](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/common_errors.llms.md): In these error messages, the code blah represents the function, object or value that the error relates to.
- [Appendix D — Some R functions you should avoid](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/functions_to_avoid.llms.md): R is very useful, but there are some R functions that are no longer the best way to get particular things done. Some of these have negative side-effects or can cause other problems. Fortunately, in every case there is a newer function that does the same thing better. Use this guide to help you avoid getting trapped by an obsolete R function.
- [Appendix E — Checklist: handling code errors](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/handling_errors.llms.md): When R code produces an error, warning or unexpected result, follow this detailed version of the four-step debugging process introduced in Chapter 8.
- [Appendix F — Chapter code library](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/chapter_code.llms.md): These completed files bring together the code developed in the book. Use the descriptions to find a starting point for your own analysis, and follow the section links in parentheses to learn how each part works. The files use the example datasets from the chapters; adapt the data sources and analytical choices to suit your own project.
- [Appendix G — Example reports and templates](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/appendices/resources.llms.md): These files provide examples to learn from and starting points for your own crime-mapping projects. You can view a finished report in your browser, or download its Quarto or R source file to see how the text and R code produce the report.
